metadata.note: The Albany and Susquehanna Railroad -- the line that made the Delaware and Hudson a railroad. Interest in a rail connection from Albany to the upper Susquehanna valley goes back to 1844, driven by the wish to reach the Pennsylvania coal fields; construction began Apr 19 1851 but the first 35 miles, Albany to Central Bridge, took twelve years and did not open until Sep 16 1863. Oneonta followed in 1865 and Binghamton in January 1869, 142 miles laid with 60-pound iron on a six-foot gauge to interchange with the Erie. Completion made it a target: Jay Gould and James Fisk fought president Joseph H. Ramsey for control through 1869 in the Susquehanna War, which ended in August with rival trains charging along the line and a brawl in a tunnel near Harpursville. J. P. Morgan settled it, and on Feb 24 1870 the road was leased to the Delaware and Hudson Canal Company for 99 years -- the deal that turned a canal company into a railroad. Run thereafter as the D&H's Susquehanna Division, it carried twelve passenger trains a day in the 1920s and was down to one round trip, trains 250 and 208, when passenger service ended in January 1963. The company was formally merged into the D&H on Jul 2 1945. Geometry here replaces a 20-point waypoint sketch that previously stood in for this corridor in cities/albany_commuter_rail.geojson; only 39 percent of the real alignment fell within 800 m of that sketch.

cities/albany_commuter_rail.geojson -- the passenger-service segmentation, the 1870s twelve-hour Albany-Binghamton running time, the 1920s figure of twelve trains a day from the D&H Rail Trail history, and the January 1963 discontinuation of trains 250 and 208 were researched for that file and are carried forward here
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Headways are estimates except the 1920s figure of twelve trains a day. Only three opening dates are established -- Central Bridge 1863, Oneonta 1865, Binghamton January 1869 -- so the intermediate railheads at Cobleskill, Worcester, Schenevus, Unadilla, Sidney and Afton are not shown as separate steps. The six-foot gauge is documented at construction but the date the line was regauged to standard is not, and no gauge change is modelled. Branches and realignments off this corridor are not drawn: the Schenectady and Susquehanna, the Cherry Valley, Sharon and Albany, the Schoharie Valley Rail Road, and the D&H's Worcester Realignment, Duanesburgh Bypass and Rotterdam Realignment are all digitized on Commons but carry no dates there and none have been sourced.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: Wednesday Sep 16 1863 opened the first completed section, Albany to Central Bridge (Schoharie Junction), with stops at Delmar, Slingerlands and New Scotland. Construction had begun Apr 19 1851 and this 35-mile stretch took twelve years -- investors, stockholders and directors wrangled over financing through the 1850s and 60s and the line inched forward as funds were secured. segments.note: The full 142-mile Albany-Binghamton line was finished and a gala excursion train from Albany was planned for Jan 12 1869. It was laid with 60-pound iron on a six-foot gauge so it could interchange freely with the Erie Railroad at Binghamton. Within months it was the prize in the Susquehanna War: Jay Gould and James Fisk, who already controlled the Erie, ran a proxy campaign through the spring and summer of 1869 against president Joseph H. Ramsey, and in August, each side holding a judicial order affirming its control, opposing trains were run at each other along the line -- Fisk seized the A&S trains at Binghamton, loaded them with Erie men and worked east taking over stations, and the two parties fought hand to hand in a tunnel near Harpursville. Frequency estimated/unsourced
